title: The Witch, The Bloom, and The Dragon's Sigh
markdown:
High on craggy peaks, wind whistling, observatories like lonely sentinels, lived Witch Mara. Her home, bubbling cauldrons and overflowing spellbooks, clung to a mule track that often vanished into mist. Her magic was a perfectly darned sock: reliable, understated, aimed at the best raspberry scones in the mountains.

Crumb, a marmot with a discerning palate, delivered opinions in emphatic chirps and tail wags. Finder of lost buttons. Nudger toward sense. He understood the mountain’s quiet whispers.

Mara’s curiosity leaped like a goat. This morning it led to a grotto rumored to hold the Whispering Bloom, said to open only when the valley pulsed with perfect harmony. A peaceful dawn chorus had carried its whispers. Humming, sporting one green sock and one striped (which utterly baffled Crumb), she plucked the bloom. It shimmered, soft warmth. As she tucked it into her satchel, a rumble deeper and more unsettled than usual.

The valley, usually a quilt of contented sheep and well-behaved yaks, felt fidgety. Sheep bristled. Mules stamped. Even stoic sherpas looked worried. The bloom, it turned out, was the valley’s peace prize. Mara had collected it. Oops.

“A bit more fuss than I’d intended. I only wanted a vibrant hue for my calming tea.”

Crumb, on a dewdrop, chittered something like: my nap schedule is in ruins.

I am calm. Less theatricality, more observation.

News reached Wizard Leofric in a spindly observatory even higher, robes a riot of peacock blue and emerald that flapped in still air. Problems demanded glitter. Subtlety was lack of sparkle.

He swept into her cottage, paused to admire himself in a polished cauldron. “A misplaced bloom? Spectacle! Dazzling illumination! Prepare for the Leofrician Luminescence!”

Mara coaxed a wilting daisy. “The valley is unsettled, not in need of a light show. You’re tracking mud on my best rug, which I enchanted to repel grime.”

“Nonsense! Dragons restless. Sighs thorny. Cosmic hiccup! I shall restore it with a flourish for the ages!”

Mara fetched her spyglass and trained it on the agitated roosts along the higher crags. Her own sighs were far less thorny. “Dragons are sensitive. Prize poodles at fireworks. This bloom is like pulling the last thread from a very important tapestry.” Crumb, who had been investigating a jam jar, paused as if to agree, then went back to the jam.

Quiet rivalry followed, as it always did when Leofric arrived with solutions already labelled. He gathered herbs that smelled like burnt toast and chanted until the teacups hummed along the dresser. Mara consulted her texts, the gossipy plants that grew in the lee of the cottage, and Crumb, who noticed what others missed: a shifted pebble, a changed wind, a marmot’s sense that the mountain was holding its breath.

“The dragons aren’t roaring. They’re grumbling. A persistent drizzle, not a thunderstorm.”

Leofric conjured a Cloud of Calming Concoctions: damp grey blanket, old socks. He sneezed dramatically. A puff splattered a mountain goat mid-thistle. Bright purple. Unbothered. Sheep bleated nervously, forming a union.

“Less theatricality, more observation! Goats are happy purple. Sheep are organizing.”

“Observation is for slugs! Magic requires pizzazz! I am the solution, and I am fabulous!”

The true complication: Mara’s empathy charm, warm thoughts around a delicate object, tuned her to Ignis, the magnificent dragon whose scales shimmered like sunsets. Not angry. Heartbroken. His sigh-clouds of mist and starlight were being ignored. A performer in an empty theatre.

“They’re exquisite. Living sculptures. No one’s noticing.”

Crumb, grooming whiskers, scampered to the sill, tiny paw at the sky. A weeping-willow sigh-cloud, opalescent, drifting unnoticed.

The bloom’s symbolism was appreciation of harmony. Ignis’s feeling of being overlooked had thrown the valley out of sync.

Leofric trudged over, goat de-lavendered to faint lilac, reputation in tatters. Mara saw his desire to be competent too. “Forget grand spells. Show Ignis his art is seen.” Crumb arranging shiny pebbles. “Your obsession with shiny things. You see the light in everything.”

Proud chirp.

“Every reflective surface. Polished shields, mica, dewdrops. Highest peaks, facing his sighing spot. When he sighs, the light will catch the clouds.”

Leofric’s eyes lit. “Symphony of reflected light! Minimal fuss, maximum impact. Surprisingly competent for odd socks.”

“And you have a flair that might organize a valley-wide treasure hunt. Those robes are easy to spot.”

I am calm. Less theatricality, more observation.

Next day the valley buzzed. Villagers, sherpas, marmots. Leofric, sparkle motivating even grumpy yaks, directed shields and mica. Vain ravens promised the shiniest bits.

Sunset came orange and purple, the kind of light that made even Leofric’s robes look almost reasonable. Ignis’s long sorrowful sigh unfurled: a wistful swan of cloud. It caught hundreds of reflectors and exploded into celestial ballet, ribbons of mist catching mica and shield-shine until the valley seemed briefly painted from the inside.

A collective gasp rose from the mule track. Ignis tilted his massive head, golden eyes wide. His overlooked art blazed. The next sigh came tentative, then opened into emerald and sapphire jewels. A resonant purr of joy ran through the mountains. Harmony restored not by power but by shared looking, a nudge to see what was always there.

Mara at her window, warmth better than raspberry scone. Crumb nudged her hand, rumble mirroring Ignis. Leofric, robes less ostentatious in twilight, joined her.

“Elegant. Next time, dispense with the lavender goat. Though it added unexpected vibrancy.”

“Memorable. The sheep are still discussing it.”

Dragons’ sighs became daily ephemeral art. Sometimes the most powerful magic was seeing the beauty already there, and helping others see it too — even the grandest creatures having the most delicate hearts, and even a marmot knowing which way to point.
characters: Mara (a witch), Crumb (a marmot), Leofric (a wizard)
audience: teenagers aged 13-15, amusing fantasy story for older readers
author: StoryGen Community
